items.stem: What is the unit of weight?
items.answer: newton (N)
items.markingKey: Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

items.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. Explain what happens to her mass and her weight on the Moon.
items.answer: Her mass stays 70 kg because the amount of matter is unchanged; her weight is less because g on the Moon is smaller.
items.markingKey: mass unchanged [1]; weight smaller due to smaller g [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a beam balance gives the same reading on the Moon as on Earth, but a newton meter does not.
items.answer: A beam balance compares the weight of the object with standard masses, and both are affected equally by g; a newton meter measures the force itself, which depends on g.
items.markingKey: balance compares with masses, g cancels [1]; newton meter measures force ∝ g [1] [2]

items.stem: An astronaut in a spacesuit has a mass of 153 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the weight.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 153 × 9.8 = 1500 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A bag of rice has a weight of 80.3 N on Mars, where g = 3.7 N/kg. Calculate its mass and its weight on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg).

An astronaut in a spacesuit with a mass of 155 kg is sent from Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to Jupiter (g = 25 N/kg). (a) State its mass on Jupiter and explain. (b) Describe how the weight of a small rock sample could be measured there with apparatus carried on the mission.
items.answer: (a) 155 kg: mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. (b) Hang it from a calibrated newton meter (spring balance) and read the force when it is still.
items.markingKey: (a) value [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) newton meter [1]; reading at equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is easier to lift a 20 kg rock on the Moon than on Earth, but just as hard to start it sliding sideways on a smooth surface.
items.answer: Lifting depends on weight, which is smaller on the Moon; starting it moving depends on mass (inertia), which is unchanged.
items.markingKey: weight smaller on Moon [1]; mass/inertia unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: An astronaut in a spacesuit has a mass of 141 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). What is the weight?
An astronaut in a spacesuit has a mass of 151 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the weight.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 151 × 9.8 = 1480 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A laboratory mass has a mass of 0.7 kg. Calculate the difference between its weight on Earth (9.8 N/kg) and on the Moon (1.6 N/kg).
items.markingKey: 6.86 N and 1.12 N [2]; difference 5.74 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg mass. What is its acceleration?
items.answer: 4 m/s²

items.stem: A car moves along a straight road at constant speed. Explain why the engine must still provide a forward force.
items.answer: Friction and air resistance act backwards; the forward force must balance them so the resultant force is zero and speed stays constant.
items.markingKey: resistive forces present [1]; forward force balances them, resultant zero [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why passengers lurch forwards when a bus brakes suddenly.
items.answer: The braking force acts on the bus, not on the passengers; by inertia (first law) their bodies continue moving forward until a force (seatbelt, seat) acts on them.
items.markingKey: inertia / first law [1]; no force on passenger initially [1] [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 1.75 kg has a resultant force of 1.1 N acting on it. Calculate the acceleration.
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 1.1/1.75 = 0.629 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.52 kg has a driving force of 4.2 N and total resistive forces of 1.2 N. Calculate the resultant force and the acceleration.

A cyclist and bicycle of mass 61 kg starts from rest. The driving force is 257 N and the resistive forces total 40 N. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Calculate the speed after 2 s. (c) Explain why, at higher speeds, the acceleration decreases even if the driving force is unchanged.
items.answer: (a) 3.56 m/s² (b) 7.11 m/s (c) air resistance increases with speed, so the resultant force decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) resultant 217 N [1]; a = 3.56 m/s² [1] (b) v = at = 7.11 m/s [1] (c) drag increases with speed, resultant smaller [1] [4]

items.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg pulls away from traffic lights in Muscat. The engine provides a forward force of 4800 N and resistive forces total 600 N. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Explain, using Newton’s third law, how the tyres produce a forward force on the car.
items.answer: (a) 4.2 m/s² (b) The tyres push backwards on the road; the road pushes forwards on the tyres with an equal force (friction).
items.markingKey: (a) a = F/m = 4200/1000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.2 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (b) tyre pushes road back [1]; road pushes car forward equally [1] [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg pulls away from traffic lights in Cape Town. The engine provides a forward force of 3000 N and resistive forces total 1000 N. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Calculate the acceleration. (c) Calculate the speed after 6 s.
items.markingKey: (a) 3000 − 1000: 2000 N [1] (b) a = F/m = 2000/1000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (c) v = at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 12 m/s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain in terms of forces why a rocket accelerates upwards at lift-off.
items.answer: Thrust from the engines is greater than its weight (and drag), so there is an upward resultant force; F = ma gives an upward acceleration.
items.markingKey: thrust > weight [1]; resultant upward gives acceleration [1] [2]

items.stem: A swimmer pushes water backwards and moves forwards. Explain this using Newton’s third law.
items.answer: The swimmer exerts a backward force on the water; the water exerts an equal and opposite (forward) force on the swimmer.
items.markingKey: force on water backwards [1]; equal opposite force on swimmer forwards [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a fully loaded lorry takes longer to reach 50 km/h than the same lorry when empty, with the same engine force.
items.answer: The loaded lorry has a greater mass, so for the same resultant force its acceleration (a = F/m) is smaller.
items.markingKey: greater mass [1]; a = F/m smaller [1] [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 1.2 kg is pulled to the right by a force of 5 N while friction of 2 N acts to the left. Calculate the acceleration of the trolley and state its direction.
items.answer: 2.5 m/s² to the right
items.markingKey: resultant = 5 − 2 = 3 N [1]; a = 3/1.2 [1] = 2.5 m/s² to the right [1] [3]

items.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg pulls away from traffic lights in Manila. The engine provides a forward force of 3000 N and resistive forces total 800 N. (a) Calculate the speed after 8 s. (b) Explain, using Newton’s third law, how the tyres produce a forward force on the car.
items.answer: (a) 17.6 m/s (b) The tyres push backwards on the road; the road pushes forwards on the tyres with an equal force (friction).
items.markingKey: (a) v = at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 17.6 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) tyre pushes road back [1]; road pushes car forward equally [1] [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 800 kg pulls away from traffic lights in Istanbul. The engine provides a forward force of 3000 N and resistive forces total 800 N. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Calculate the speed after 4 s. (c) Later the car travels at a steady speed. State the size of the driving force then, if the resistive forces have risen to 3000 N, and explain.
items.answer: (a) 2.75 m/s² (b) 11 m/s (c) 3000 N: constant speed means zero resultant force.
items.markingKey: (a) a = F/m = 2200/800 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.75 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (b) v = at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 11 m/s with unit [1] [2] (c) value [1]; balanced forces [1] [2]

items.stem: Friction always acts …
options: in the opposite direction to the motion (or attempted motion)
towards the centre of the Earth
items.answer: in the opposite direction to the motion (or attempted motion)
items.markingKey: Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces.

items.stem: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Explain why her acceleration decreases as she falls.
items.answer: As her speed increases, air resistance increases; the resultant force (weight − air resistance) decreases, so a = F/m decreases.
items.markingKey: drag increases with speed [1]; resultant force decreases [1]; a = F/m [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a skydiver slows down when the parachute opens.
items.answer: The parachute greatly increases surface area, so air resistance becomes larger than weight; the resultant force is upwards so she decelerates.
items.markingKey: larger area → more drag [1]; drag > weight, upward resultant [1] [2]

items.stem: A base jumper of total mass 75 kg is falling. At one instant the air resistance is 184 N (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the resultant force.
items.markingKey: W = 735 N; resultant = 735 − 184 = 551 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A parachuted supply crate of total mass 60 kg is falling. At one instant the air resistance is 118 N (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the acceleration at this instant.
items.answer: 7.83 m/s² downwards

items.stem: A skydiver of total mass 75 kg jumps from a helicopter above Lisbon. (g = 9.8 N/kg) (a) Explain why the acceleration decreases as the speed increases. (b) State and explain one way the skydiver can increase her terminal velocity.
items.answer: (a) Air resistance increases, so resultant force (W − drag) decreases; a = F/m. (b) Dive head-first/tuck in to reduce area, reducing drag at each speed.
items.markingKey: (a) Air resistance increases [1]; so resultant force (W − drag) decreases, a = F/m [1] [2] (b) Dive head-first/tuck in to reduce area [1]; reducing drag at each speed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a parachutist reaches a new, lower terminal velocity after the parachute opens.
items.answer: As she slows, drag decreases until it equals her weight again; the forces balance at a lower speed because of the larger area.
items.markingKey: drag decreases as speed falls [1]; balances weight at lower speed [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho records the speed of a falling object every second: time/s = 0, 1, 2, …, 9; speed/m/s = 0, 9.9, 18.2, 24.2, 28.1, 30.3, 31.4, 31.9, 31.9, 31.9. (a) State the terminal velocity. (b) Calculate the average acceleration in the first second. (c) Explain why the speed stops increasing.
items.answer: (a) 31.9 m/s (b) 9.9 m/s² (c) air resistance rises with speed until it equals the weight; resultant force zero.
items.markingKey: (a) 31.9 m/s [1] (b) 9.9 m/s² [1] (c) drag balances weight [1] [3]

items.stem: A parachuted supply crate of total mass 120 kg (g = 9.8 N/kg) falls at terminal velocity. The parachute then opens and the air resistance immediately becomes 2940 N. (a) State the air resistance just before the parachute opens. (b) Calculate the deceleration just after it opens. (c) Describe what happens to the speed and the air resistance after this until a new steady state is reached.
items.answer: (a) 1180 N (b) 14.7 m/s² (c) speed decreases, so air resistance decreases until it equals the weight again; new lower terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: (a) equals weight = 1180 N [1] (b) resultant = 2940 − 1180 = 1760 N upwards [1]; a = 14.7 m/s² [1] (c) speed and drag decrease [1]; lower terminal velocity when drag = weight [1] [5]

items.stem: A wingsuit flyer of mass 90 kg jumps from a cliff. (g = 9.8 N/kg) (a) State the acceleration at the moment of jumping and explain. (b) State and explain one way the skydiver can increase her terminal velocity.
items.answer: (a) 9.8 m/s²: speed is zero so there is no air resistance. (b) Dive head-first/tuck in to reduce area, reducing drag at each speed.
items.markingKey: (a) value [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) Dive head-first/tuck in to reduce area [1]; reducing drag at each speed [1] [2]

items.stem: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In which direction is the resultant force on it?
options: Zero, because the speed is constant
Towards the centre of the circle
items.answer: Towards the centre of the circle
items.markingKey: A force perpendicular to the velocity, towards the centre, changes direction but not speed.

items.stem: What provides the force towards the centre for a satellite orbiting the Earth?
items.answer: Gravity (the Earth’s gravitational pull)
items.markingKey: Gravitational attraction acts towards Earth’s centre.

items.stem: Explain why a car can skid off a wet, icy bend if it goes too fast.
items.answer: A larger speed needs a larger force towards the centre; on ice the friction cannot provide enough, so the car moves in a wider path (straight on).
items.markingKey: faster needs bigger centripetal force [1]; friction too small on ice [1] [2]

items.stem: A student whirls a bung of mass 100 g on a string in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m and measures the tension needed at different speeds: speed/m/s 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; tension/N 1.6, 3.6, 6.4. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether the tension needed at 3.0 m/s would be larger or smaller for a radius of 1.0 m.
items.answer: (a) The force needed increases as speed increases (more than proportionally). (b) Smaller: a larger radius needs a smaller force for the same speed and mass.
items.markingKey: (a) trend [1]; not proportional/increases faster [1] (b) smaller with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a passenger on a fairground carousel, moving at a steady speed in a circle. (a) Describe what would happen if this force suddenly stopped acting. (b) State one way of keeping the same force but making the object move faster.
items.answer: (a) It would move off in a straight line along the tangent at constant speed. (b) Increase the radius of the circle (or reduce the mass).
items.markingKey: (a) straight line [1]; tangent [1] [2] (b) Increase the radius of the circle (or reduce the mass) [1]

items.stem: What provides the force towards the centre when a car drives round a bend?
options: Friction between the tyres and the road
items.answer: Friction between the tyres and the road
items.markingKey: Sideways friction on the tyres.

items.stem: A student whirls a bung of mass 50 g on a string in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m and measures the tension needed at different speeds: speed/m/s 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; tension/N 0.6, 1.35, 2.4. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether the tension needed at 3.0 m/s would be larger or smaller for a radius of 1.0 m.
items.answer: (a) The force needed increases as speed increases (more than proportionally). (b) Smaller: a larger radius needs a smaller force for the same speed and mass.
items.markingKey: (a) trend [1]; not proportional/increases faster [1] (b) smaller with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: What is the unit of momentum?
items.answer: kg m/s
items.markingKey: p = mv: kg × m/s.

items.stem: Explain how the crumple zone of a car reduces the force on the passengers in a crash.
items.answer: The crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop; the change in momentum is the same, so the force (Δp/Δt) is smaller.
items.markingKey: longer time [1]; same Δp so smaller F = Δp/Δt [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a gun recoils when it fires a bullet.
items.answer: Total momentum before is zero; after, the bullet has forward momentum, so the gun must have equal momentum backwards to keep the total zero.
items.markingKey: initial momentum zero [1]; equal and opposite momentum [1] [2]

items.stem: A football of mass 0.43 kg moves at 10.4 m/s. Calculate the momentum.
items.answer: 4.47 kg m/s
items.markingKey: p = mv = 0.43 × 10.4 = 4.47 kg m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A football of mass 0.43 kg has a momentum of 4.47 kg m/s. Calculate its speed and its kinetic energy.

A trolley of mass 3 kg moving at 5 m/s to the right collides head-on with a trolley of mass 1.5 kg moving at 2 m/s to the left. They stick together. (a) Calculate the total momentum before the collision. (b) Calculate the velocity just after the collision. (c) Calculate the kinetic energy lost.
items.answer: (a) 12 kg m/s to the right (b) 2.67 m/s to the right (c) 24.5 J
items.markingKey: (a) 3×5 − 1.5×2 = 12 kg m/s (signs) [2] (b) ÷ 4.5 = 2.67 m/s with direction [1] (c) KE before − after = 24.5 J [1] [4]

items.stem: A cannon of mass 1000 kg, mounted on a frictionless track, fires a cannonball of mass 5 kg forwards at 200 m/s. Both are initially at rest. (a) Calculate the recoil speed of the cannon. (b) The cannonball is accelerated for 0.002 s. Calculate the average force on it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1000 = 1000 × v [1]; v = 1 m/s [1] [2] (b) F = Δp/Δt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 500 000 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A toy spring launcher of mass 0.5 kg fires a ball bearing of mass 0.03 kg forwards at 6 m/s. Both are initially at rest. (a) State the total momentum before firing. (b) Explain why the recoil speed is much smaller than the speed of the ball bearing. (c) The ball bearing is accelerated for 0.05 s. Calculate the average force on it.
items.answer: (a) 0 (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass, so smaller speed. (c) 3.6 N
items.markingKey: (a) 0 [1] (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass [1]; so smaller speed [1] [2] (c) F = Δp/Δt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.6 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Impulse is equal to …
items.answer: force × time (the change in momentum)
items.markingKey: Impulse = FΔt = Δ(mv).

items.stem: Explain why a gymnast bends her knees when landing.
items.answer: Bending the knees increases the time to stop; for the same change in momentum the force on her legs is smaller.
items.markingKey: longer time [1]; smaller force for same Δp [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why momentum is a vector quantity and how this matters in a head-on collision.
items.answer: Momentum has direction (velocity is a vector); momenta in opposite directions must be given opposite signs, so they can partly cancel.
items.markingKey: direction from velocity [1]; opposite signs / can cancel [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why airbags and seat belts are designed to stretch or deflate slightly in a crash.
items.answer: They extend the stopping time of the passenger, reducing the force for the same change in momentum, and spread the force over a larger area.
items.markingKey: longer time [1]; smaller force [1] [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 1.5 kg moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 2 kg and they stick together. Determine the speed of the joined trolleys just after the collision.
items.markingKey: 1.5 × 3 = (1.5 + 2)v; v = 4.5/3.5 = 1.29 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A cannon of mass 1000 kg, mounted on a frictionless track, fires a cannonball of mass 8 kg forwards at 150 m/s. Both are initially at rest. (a) Calculate the recoil speed of the cannon. (b) Explain why the recoil speed is much smaller than the speed of the cannonball.
items.answer: (a) 1.2 m/s (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass, so smaller speed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1200 = 1000 × v [1]; v = 1.2 m/s [1] [2] (b) Equal momentum but much larger mass [1]; so smaller speed [1] [2]

items.stem: Which statement about mass and weight is correct?
options: Mass and weight are the same thing
Weight is the same everywhere; mass depends on gravity
Mass is the same everywhere; weight depends on gravitational field strength
items.answer: Mass is the same everywhere; weight depends on gravitational field strength
items.markingKey: Mass = amount of matter; weight = gravitational force = mg.

items.stem: Describe the gravitational field near the Earth’s surface and explain the meaning of g = 9.8 N/kg.
items.answer: Each kilogram of mass experiences a gravitational force of 9.8 N directed towards the centre of the Earth.
items.markingKey: force per kg [1]; directed towards Earth’s centre [1] [2]

items.stem: A car has a mass of 901 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the weight.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 901 × 9.8 = 8830 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A robot rover with a mass of 709 kg is sent from Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). (a) Calculate its weight on Earth. (b) State its mass on the Moon and explain. (c) Explain why a smaller rocket force is needed to lift it off the surface of the Moon than of Earth.
items.answer: (a) 6950 N (b) 709 kg: mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. (c) Its weight there is smaller, so less upward force is needed to give a resultant upward force.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg = 709 × 9.8 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6950 N with unit [1] [2] (b) value [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) weight comparison [1]; link to required upward force [1] [2]

items.stem: An object moves at a constant velocity. What is the resultant force on it?
items.answer: Zero
items.markingKey: Newton’s first law: constant velocity ⇒ balanced forces.

items.stem: For a hammer hitting a nail, one force is: "the hammer pushes the nail into the wood". State the Newton’s third law partner of this force and give two ways in which the two forces are the same.
items.answer: The nail pushes back on the hammer. They are equal in size, of the same type, act along the same line (but in opposite directions on different objects).
items.markingKey: partner force [1]; any two of: equal size, same type, same line [2] [3]

items.stem: A lorry of mass 12 700 kg has a resultant force of 22 700 N acting on it. Work out the acceleration.
items.markingKey: a = F/m = 22 700/12 700 = 1.79 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.5 kg is pulled to the right by a force of 2 N while friction of 1 N acts to the left. Calculate the acceleration of the trolley and state its direction.
items.answer: 2 m/s² to the right
items.markingKey: resultant = 2 − 1 = 1 N [1]; a = 1/0.5 [1] = 2 m/s² to the right [1] [3]

items.stem: An electric taxi of mass 1500 kg accelerates from rest. The driving force is 4800 N; friction and air resistance together are 600 N. (a) Calculate the speed after 6 s. (b) Later the car travels at a steady speed. State the size of the driving force then, if the resistive forces have risen to 4800 N, and explain.
items.answer: (a) 16.8 m/s (b) 4800 N: constant speed means zero resultant force.
items.markingKey: (a) v = at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 16.8 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) value [1]; balanced forces [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State one useful effect and one problem caused by friction. (b) A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?
items.answer: (a) Useful: grip of tyres/shoes, brakes. Problem: wear, heating, wasted energy in machines. (b) Air resistance equals weight
items.markingKey: (a) useful [1]; problem [1] [2] (b) At terminal velocity forces are balanced, resultant force zero.

items.stem: Explain why cyclists crouch low over the handlebars in a race.
items.answer: Smaller frontal area means less air resistance, so for the same force they reach a higher top speed.
items.markingKey: less area → less drag [1]; higher speed / less energy [1] [2]

items.stem: A parachuted supply crate of total mass 70 kg is falling. At one instant the air resistance is 343 N (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the resultant force.
items.markingKey: W = 686 N; resultant = 686 − 343 = 343 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A hammer thrower spins a heavy ball on a wire. Explain why the force needed in the wire is larger for a heavier ball at the same speed and radius.
items.answer: A larger mass needs a larger force towards the centre to keep it moving in the same circle at the same speed.
items.markingKey: greater mass [1]; larger force needed for same speed and radius [1] [2]

items.stem: A student whirls a bung of mass 50 g on a string in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m and measures the tension needed at different speeds: speed/m/s 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; tension/N 0.4, 0.9, 1.6. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether the tension needed at 3.0 m/s would be larger or smaller for a radius of 1.0 m.
items.answer: (a) The force needed increases as speed increases (more than proportionally). (b) Smaller: a larger radius needs a smaller force for the same speed and mass.
items.markingKey: (a) trend [1]; not proportional/increases faster [1] (b) smaller with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a cyclist going round a curved track, moving at a steady speed in a circle. (a) Explain why the object is accelerating even if its speed is constant. (b) State how the force must change if the speed increases but the radius stays the same. (c) State one way of keeping the same force but making the object move faster.
items.answer: (a) Velocity is a vector; its direction keeps changing. (b) It must increase. (c) Increase the radius of the circle (or reduce the mass).
items.markingKey: (a) Velocity is a vector [1]; its direction keeps changing [1] [2] (b) It must increase [1] (c) Increase the radius of the circle (or reduce the mass) [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why momentum is a vector quantity and how this matters in a head-on collision. (b) Explain why a gymnast bends her knees when landing.
items.answer: (a) Momentum has direction (velocity is a vector); momenta in opposite directions must be given opposite signs, so they can partly cancel. (b) Bending the knees increases the time to stop; for the same change in momentum the force on her legs is smaller.
items.markingKey: (a) direction from velocity [1]; opposite signs / can cancel [1] [2] (b) longer time [1]; smaller force for same Δp [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why momentum is a vector quantity and how this matters in a head-on collision. (b) Explain why a gymnast bends her knees when landing.
items.answer: (a) Momentum has direction (velocity is a vector); momenta in opposite directions must be given opposite signs, so they can partly cancel. (b) Bending the knees increases the time to stop; for the same change in momentum the force on her legs is smaller.
items.markingKey: (a) direction from velocity [1]; opposite signs / can cancel [1] [2] (b) longer time [1]; smaller force for same Δp [1] [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 1 kg moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 0.5 kg and they stick together. Work out the speed of the joined trolleys just after the collision.
items.answer: 2 m/s
items.markingKey: 1 × 3 = (1 + 0.5)v; v = 3/1.5 = 2 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tennis racket hits a ball of mass 0.058 kg, initially at rest, so that it leaves at 23 m/s. The contact time is 0.005 s. Calculate the average force.

A rifle of mass 5 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.01 kg forwards at 400 m/s. Both are initially at rest. (a) State the total momentum before firing. (b) Calculate the recoil speed of the rifle. (c) The bullet is accelerated for 0.002 s. Calculate the average force on it.
items.markingKey: (a) 0 [1] (b) 4 = 5 × v [1]; v = 0.8 m/s [1] [2] (c) F = Δp/Δt (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2000 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the weight of a 2.0 kg bag on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg)?

A student studies how the weight of an object depends on mass and gravity. The gravitational field strength is multiplied by 5 while the mass stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the weight changes.
items.answer: The weight becomes 5 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using W = mg: weight ∝ gravitational field strength; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A suitcase has a mass of 21 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Determine the weight.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 21 × 9.8 = 206 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A suitcase with a mass of 23 kg is sent from Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) to Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg). (a) Calculate its weight on Earth. (b) State its mass on Mars and explain. (c) Describe how the weight of a small rock sample could be measured there with apparatus carried on the mission.
items.answer: (a) 225 N (b) 23 kg: mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. (c) Hang it from a calibrated newton meter (spring balance) and read the force when it is still.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg = 23 × 9.8 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 225 N with unit [1] [2] (b) value [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) newton meter [1]; reading at equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation links resultant force, mass and acceleration?
items.answer: F = ma
items.markingKey: Newton’s second law.

items.stem: For a gun firing a bullet, one force is: "the gun pushes the bullet forwards". State the Newton’s third law partner of this force and give two ways in which the two forces are the same.
items.answer: The bullet pushes the gun backwards (recoil). They are equal in size, of the same type, act along the same line (but in opposite directions on different objects).
items.markingKey: partner force [1]; any two of: equal size, same type, same line [2] [3]

items.stem: A rocket of mass 39 800 kg accelerates at 9.44 m/s². Determine the resultant force.
items.markingKey: F = ma = 39 800 × 9.44 = 376 000 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1190 kg has a driving force of 5780 N and total resistive forces of 1160 N. Calculate the resultant force and the acceleration.

A car of mass 1000 kg pulls away from traffic lights in Lima. The engine provides a forward force of 3600 N and resistive forces total 600 N. (a) Calculate the speed after 6 s. (b) Four passengers with total mass 300 kg get in. Calculate the new initial acceleration with the same forces.
items.markingKey: (a) v = at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 18 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) 3000/1300 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.31 m/s² with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State one useful effect and one problem caused by friction. (b) Which change reduces friction between two surfaces?
items.answer: (a) Useful: grip of tyres/shoes, brakes. Problem: wear, heating, wasted energy in machines. (b) Adding a lubricant such as oil
items.markingKey: (a) useful [1]; problem [1] [2] (b) Lubricants separate the surfaces.

items.stem: Explain why a car’s top speed is limited even when the engine gives its maximum force.
items.answer: Air resistance increases with speed until it (with friction) equals the maximum driving force; then the resultant force is zero and the car cannot accelerate further.
items.markingKey: drag increases with speed [1]; balances max driving force, zero resultant [1] [2]

items.stem: A parachuted supply crate of total mass 100 kg is falling. At one instant the air resistance is 245 N (g = 9.8 N/kg). Work out the resultant force.
items.markingKey: W = 980 N; resultant = 980 − 245 = 735 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Explain why the speed of an object moving in a circle does not change, even though a force acts on it.
items.answer: The force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed.
items.markingKey: force perpendicular to motion [1]; changes direction only [1] [2]

items.stem: A student whirls a bung of mass 100 g on a string in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m and measures the tension needed at different speeds: speed/m/s 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; tension/N 1.2, 2.7, 4.8. (a) Describe the trend. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether the tension needed at 3.0 m/s would be larger or smaller for a radius of 1.0 m.
items.answer: (a) The force needed increases as speed increases (more than proportionally). (b) Smaller: a larger radius needs a smaller force for the same speed and mass.
items.markingKey: (a) trend [1]; not proportional/increases faster [1] (b) smaller with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a passenger on a fairground carousel, moving at a steady speed in a circle. (a) Name the force that provides it. (b) Explain why the object is accelerating even if its speed is constant. (c) State how the force must change if the speed increases but the radius stays the same.
items.answer: (a) The push of the seat and the chain tension. (b) Velocity is a vector; its direction keeps changing. (c) It must increase.
items.markingKey: (a) The push of the seat and the chain tension [1] (b) Velocity is a vector [1]; its direction keeps changing [1] [2] (c) It must increase [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a gun recoils when it fires a bullet. (b) Explain why airbags and seat belts are designed to stretch or deflate slightly in a crash.
items.answer: (a) Total momentum before is zero; after, the bullet has forward momentum, so the gun must have equal momentum backwards to keep the total zero. (b) They extend the stopping time of the passenger, reducing the force for the same change in momentum, and spread the force over a larger area.
items.markingKey: (a) initial momentum zero [1]; equal and opposite momentum [1] [2] (b) longer time [1]; smaller force [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the crumple zone of a car reduces the force on the passengers in a crash. (b) Explain why momentum is a vector quantity and how this matters in a head-on collision.
items.answer: (a) The crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop; the change in momentum is the same, so the force (Δp/Δt) is smaller. (b) Momentum has direction (velocity is a vector); momenta in opposite directions must be given opposite signs, so they can partly cancel.
items.markingKey: (a) longer time [1]; same Δp so smaller F = Δp/Δt [1] [2] (b) direction from velocity [1]; opposite signs / can cancel [1] [2]

items.stem: A golf club strikes a stationary ball of mass 0.046 kg so that it leaves at 39 m/s. The contact time is 0.0005 s. Determine the change in momentum (impulse).
items.answer: 1.79 kg m/s
items.markingKey: Δp = m Δv = 0.046 × 39 = 1.79 kg m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A bowling ball of mass 6 kg has a momentum of 32.4 kg m/s. Calculate its speed and its kinetic energy.
